extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, attorneys and respondents in USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) proceedings; OED/USPTO counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria used by the USPTO/OED and the Administrative Law Judge to evaluate practitioner misconduct, determine violations of the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct, and select appropriate sanctions (including exclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to hear proceeding (jurisdiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: This Court is authorized to hear this proceeding and to issue this Initial Decision pursuant to 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.19 and 11.39.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative Law Judges (under an interagency agreement) have authority to hear USPTO disciplinary cases; confirm statutory/regulatory citations before proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service on counsel requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a respondent is known to be represented by an attorney, service of the complaint is required to be made upon the attorney only. (37 C.F.R. § 11.35(c)). For other papers, the requirement for service on Respondent's attorney is the same. (37 C.F.R. § 11.42(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper service on the attorney of record establishes constructive service upon the respondent; retain proof of certified mailing and track return receipts. Failure to serve correctly may affect later default findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of failure to timely answer / default rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to timely file an answer constitutes an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in a default judgment. (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If respondent does not file a timely answer, allegations may be deemed admitted and the OED may move for default judgment; a defaulted respondent generally waives opportunity to contest facts or state of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to notify client of significant correspondence (§10.23(c)(8))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not 'fail[] to inform a client or former client or fail[] to timely notify the Office of an inability to notify a client or former client of correspondence received from the Office or the client's or former client's opponent in an inter partes proceeding before the Office when the correspondence (i) could have a significant effect on a matter pending before the Office, (ii) is received by the practitioner on behalf of a client or former client and (iii) is correspondence of which a reasonable practitioner would believe under the circumstances the client or former client should be notified.' (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(8)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three elements must be considered: (i) significance to the pending matter, (ii) correspondence received on behalf of client, and (iii) whether a reasonable practitioner would notify the client. Examples in the decision: Notices to File Missing Parts, non-final Office actions, and Notices of Abandonment—failure to inform clients of such correspondence violated this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on disreputable or gross misconduct (§10.23(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not 'engage in disreputable or gross misconduct.' (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated abandonment of clients' matters, taking payment without performing required legal services, and ignoring clients' inquiries are examples supporting a finding of disreputable/gross misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (§10.23(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not 'engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.' (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct that undermines the patent system or public confidence in practitioners (e.g., failing to pursue prosecution such that clients' rights are lost) falls within this proscription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect of a legal matter (§10.77(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not '[n]eglect a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner.' (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to respond to Office communications, abandoning patent applications without client knowledge or consent, and ignoring client communications constitute neglect under this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentional or habitual violation of USPTO rules (§10.89(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner is proscribed from 'intentionally or habitually violating the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility.' (37 C.F.R. § 10.89(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated patterns of the same misconduct (e.g., multiple matters where Notices to File Missing Parts and Office actions were ignored) support finding of intentional or habitual violation rather than isolated malpractice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other conduct adversely reflecting on fitness (§10.23(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may not 'engage in any other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the [USPTO].' (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule is broad but requires specific allegation/evidence; absence of an allegation means no basis to find a violation under this subsection (see decision noting no such allegation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing requirements: basic filing fee and oath/declaration (37 C.F.R. §1.63) / Notices to File Missing Parts
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO practice requires the statutory basic filing fee and an oath or declaration under 37 C.F.R. § 1.63; omission triggers a Notice to File Missing Parts and, if not corrected, may lead to abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must ensure applications include required fees and declarations; Notices to File Missing Parts are formal warnings—practitioners must forward notices to clients and correct omissions or risk abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to respond to Office actions (reply periods and abandonment warnings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-final Office actions set a period for reply (e.g., three months) and warn that failure to reply will cause the application to become abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must monitor correspondence, timely prepare responses within the reply window, and promptly inform clients of communications that could trigger abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions framework (37 C.F.R. §11.54(b)) — four sentencing factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Before excluding a practitioner from practice, the Court must consider four factors (if applicable): (1) Did the practitioner violate a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession? (2) Did the practitioner act intentionally, knowingly, or negligently? (3) What amount of actual or potential injury was caused? (4) Are there any aggravating or mitigating factors? (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each factor is weighed: violations of duty, deliberate misconduct, and substantial actual/potential injury all support harsher sanctions. The presence of aggravating factors can justify maximum sanctions such as exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors relevant to sanction severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors cited include: practitioner's long experience (twenty years) and awareness of obligations; pattern of misconduct (multiple client matters abandoned); failure to repair errors (no refunds, no cures); and prior disciplinary record (prior suspension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A combination of experience, repeated conduct, failure to remedy, and prior discipline strongly support exclusion or the maximum sanction. Lack of mitigating evidence may further support exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference of intent from failure to participate
rubrics_metrics.description: When a respondent fails to participate or file an answer, the respondent 'waived the opportunity to contest the USPTO's assertions as to his state of mind' and the court may conclude actions were deliberate based on the record and admissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonparticipation can justify findings of intent or deliberate conduct when circumstantial evidence (e.g., undelivered mail not returned, emails not undeliverable, repeated similar incidents) supports such an inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy available for professional misconduct: exclusion from practice
rubrics_metrics.description: One available sanction for severe or repeated misconduct is exclusion from practice before the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (i.e., disbarment from USPTO practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusion is ordered after analyzing the four §11.54(b) factors and finding violations, intent, injury, and aggravating circumstances sufficient to warrant the penalty.
